title: Know Your Destination: Backwards Design and Writing
author: Bob Sparks
summary: Bob Sparks, a high school English teacher, argues that backward design, starting from the culminating task and working back to the skills it requires, is the most reliable way to plan writing instruction. He opens with a road-trip analogy to make the case that a course, unit or lesson needs a known destination before the route is chosen. He then walks through his own rhetoric unit, where students read texts such as Gandhi and King and write at increasing levels of difficulty along the way. Those stops run from gist statements to a summary paragraph, rhetorical explanations, evidence-based text questions and finally an analysis paragraph. The sequence is scaffolded with modeling and gradual release, and it builds stamina for a full argumentative or informative essay. The piece is a practical teacher-voice example rather than a research argument, but it shows concretely how end-goal planning turns writing into a chain of small, practiced tasks. Sparks adds that the approach adapts to middle and elementary classrooms.
points: Backward design means starting from the standards-aligned culminating task, identifying the knowledge and skills needed for mastery, then embedding those elements throughout the unit.
Sparks sequences writing tasks from gist statements to summary paragraph to rhetorical explanation to analysis paragraph, so each task rehearses a piece of the final essay.
Modeling by thinking aloud, partner work and templates are used to vary scaffolding by student readiness.
The analysis paragraph, built on a framework such as SOAPStone, serves as deliberate practice for the body paragraph of a full essay.
The approach is not limited to high school, since the same stepwise structure can be shrunk for shorter tasks in middle or elementary classrooms.
quotes: Considering where you are going is essential when planning any kind of journey. The same is true for the academic journey you may be preparing to lead students on throughout a course, a semester, a unit, or simply a lesson.

One principle of instructional design that I have held to closely is that of backward design. Backward design essentially means beginning with the end in mind—considering the standards and instructional objectives for an entire lesson or unit and working backwards to plan assessments, activities, and tasks to ensure students are able to master those objectives.

As a high school English teacher focused on growing students’ literacy skills and improving college readiness, teaching my students how to write extended responses and various types of essays is essential. Yet my students come to me with a variety of levels of readiness and stamina for these tasks. In order to prepare them to write a complete and effective essay, I have to work backwards from this goal and embed the necessary skills and content along the way to prepare them and build their writing stamina.
With each successive read of a text, I embed writing tasks. During the first read, we write gist statements of each significant section of the text.

Finally, drawing on the close reading and text-based questions, students will write some form of literary or textual analysis paragraph using a framework, such as a SOAPStone. This paragraph is essentially a form of practice for writing a body paragraph of an informative or argumentative essay, requiring students to have a clear topic sentence and appropriately embedded evidence.

While I am writing from my context in a high school English classroom, this approach and its scaffolded components could be adapted to shorter writing tasks and texts in a middle or even elementary classroom. The key is knowing where you want your students to go with their writing and planning out the discreet skills, strategies, and tasks along the way to get them there.

By the time students have worked through the texts and written at various levels—gist statements, summary paragraphs, rhetorical explanations, responses to questions, and an analysis paragraph—they are prepared for an essay or extended writing assignment.
